## Coverage note

Read slice in full (L1 through end). Hamilton’s running translation + verse-by-verse commentary for Gen 31–36, including one **New Testament Appropriation** block after Gen 33 (John 4 / Acts 7). No material beyond ch. 36 in this range. Philological footnotes dense on *terāpîm*, *paḥaḏ yiṣḥāq*, *śārâ/yiśrā’ēl*, *minḥâ*, *neḇālâ*, Edomite lists; extract below prioritizes load-bearing theological, ethical, and narrative claims with verbatim anchors.

## Claims

### C-V2R4-01 | Yahweh’s return command; Laban’s face vs God’s “with you”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Jacob’s flight is driven not by fright alone but by Yahweh’s directive to return home with the promise of presence. Laban’s *face* is no longer *with* Jacob (v. 2), while Yahweh says “I will be with you” (v. 3)—same promise as when Jacob fled Canaan (28:15a). Whether leaving or returning, Jacob does not travel alone.
- **Quote:** “Still, it is not fright or intuition that drives Jacob back to Canaan, but a directive from Yahweh. … Whether leaving his home or returning to it, Jacob does not travel alone. … ʿimmô (with a negative) tells us about Laban and Jacob. ʿimmāk (a positive) tells us about Yahweh and Jacob.”
- **Locus:** on 31:1–3; slice ~L42–46
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[jacob]], [[divine-providence]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R4-02 | Ch. 31 as sobered theology of flock wealth (vs ch. 30 craft)
- **Claim:** Jacob’s explanation to the wives of how he gained flocks does not contradict ch. 30 (crafty sympathetic magic). Ch. 31 is hindsight: with sobered reflection Jacob attributes increment to God’s overruling of Laban’s ten wage-changes; dream data (vv. 12–13a) are novel relative to ch. 30.
- **Quote:** “Jacob’s explanation of the size of his own flocks to his wives does not contradict that told in the previous chapter … Jacob’s explanation here represents his sobered reflections on the happenings of the last several years. With hindsight, he is able to put the increment of his flocks in proper perspective.” / “He is making clear to them that he did not dupe Laban out of his flocks by magic or trickery.”
- **Locus:** on 31:4–13; slice ~L48–54
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[rachel]], [[leah]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-03 | Rachel and Leah’s grievance: sold, no patrimony
- **Claim:** Wives support departure because of what Laban did *to them*, not only to Jacob: sold as foreign women; bride-price / succession money “devoured.” Hamilton notes early-Israel bride-price reversion possibilities and Van Seters’s Neo-Assyrian purchase parallel, but cautions that Gen 31 lacks explicit money payment and *māḵar* may be analogical protest, not firm legal custom.
- **Quote:** “If Jacob thinks he needs to convince his wives, he is wrong. They already believe him and are prepared to support him, not because of what Laban has done to Jacob, but because of what Laban has done to them.” / “‘a protest of indignant women is no evidence of legal custom.’”
- **Locus:** on 31:14–16; slice ~L56–58
- **Targets:** [[rachel]], [[leah]], [[jacob]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-04 | Narrator’s legitimacy of Jacob’s livestock
- **Claim:** On departure the narrator stresses Jacob’s animals as legitimately *acquired* (*rāḵaš*), via repeated third-person suffixes and double “that he acquired”—not swindled.
- **Quote:** “The livestock which Jacob takes are not animals that he has swindled from Laban. They are livestock he has acquired (rāḵaš) legitimately, says the narrator.”
- **Locus:** on 31:17–18; slice ~L78–79
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-05 | Teraphim: household gods; etymology; size; “godnapping”
- **Claim:** Rachel steals *terāpîm* (Laban/Jacob: “my/the gods”)—portable household gods concealable in a camel saddle, contrast larger 1 Sam 19 teraphim. Etymology uncertain (rags / interpreters / Hittite *tarpiš* spirit / healers from *rāpāʾ*); third and fourth most likely, none convincing. Narrator’s sarcasm: can one steal gods?—“godnapping.”
- **Quote:** “The story in Gen. 31 never comments on Rachel’s ability to steal her father’s household gods. From a Hebrew perspective, of course, one might ask: ‘Can one steal gods?’ … The ancient reader would not miss the sarcasm in this story, for here is a new crime — ‘godnapping’!” / “Thus they are clearly household gods, rather than temple gods, probably small and obviously portable”
- **Locus:** on 31:19; slice ~L81–93
- **Targets:** [[rachel]], [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R4-06 | Motive for theft: Nuzi challenged; protection / spite; Emar; text silent
- **Claim:** Against Nuzi-inheritance-title readings (Rachel securing heirship for Jacob), Hamilton follows Greenberg and others: possession of gods ≠ automatic inheritance claim; plan makes little sense if permanently leaving. Simpler: protection on journey; or greed/spite—Rachel, once “stolen” from Jacob by Laban’s switch, now steals Laban’s objects of desire. Emar wills re-open heirship/gods links but distinctions remain; Rachel’s scheme is hasty. **Text represses motives**; only circumstances (sheepshearing) are narrated.
- **Quote:** “A simpler explanation is that Rachel possibly stole the hearth gods for protection on her journey to Canaan.” / “Now the tables are turned: it is Rachel who steals from Laban the objects of his desire. But the text represses any mention or explanation of Rachel’s motives.”
- **Locus:** on 31:19; slice ~L95–109
- **Targets:** [[rachel]], [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[victor-hamilton]]

### C-V2R4-07 | *gānaḇ* sevenfold: Rachel’s real theft vs Jacob’s figurative “stole Laban’s heart”
- **Claim:** *gānaḇ* appears seven times in ch. 31. Rachel’s theft is literal; Jacob “stole Laban’s heart” (deception by flight) is figurative self-defense. Juxtaposition makes Jacob’s deception seem less serious than Rachel’s. Laban as “Aramean” after himself being duped echoes *rāmâ*/Aramean sound-play from 29:25.
- **Quote:** “Rachel perpetrated an actual theft, while Jacob’s theft is an act of self-defense and reasonable. Hers is unexplained and appears to be arbitrary. The juxtapositioning of the two acts of thievery in this way creates the impression that Jacob’s deception is not as serious as Rachel’s.”
- **Locus:** on 31:19–21; slice ~L84–85, L110–112
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[rachel]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-08 | Pursuit, dream restraint, Laban as plaintiff; gods charge more serious
- **Claim:** Laban pursues seven days (nonliteral pace problem noted) to Gilead; God warns in a dream not to “speak from good unto evil”—not total silence but no prosecuting legal action. Laban’s daughter-captive charge is **untrue** (daughters left voluntarily, 31:14–16). Second charge (“why steal my gods?”) is briefer but **more serious**: Laban respected Jacob’s God; Jacob has not respected Laban’s gods. Death-oath of 31:32 is hyperbole—not safe legal source for sancta death penalty.
- **Quote:** “Rather, even if he feels that he has a legitimate grievance, Laban is not to prosecute and take (legal) action against Jacob. ‘God has corked the bottle of his aggressiveness.’” / “Nonetheless, it is more likely that Laban’s second charge against Jacob is the more serious one. Laban respected Jacob’s God, but Jacob has not respected Laban’s gods.” / “‘drawing legal ruling from possible hyperbole in narrative speech is a precarious enterprise.’”
- **Locus:** on 31:22–32; slice ~L151–180
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[rachel]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-09 | Rachel sits on gods; menstrual excuse; gods as “sanitary towels”
- **Claim:** Search uses *nāšaš* (echo of Isaac “feeling” Jacob, 27:21–22). Gods small enough to sit on; menstrual claim prevents rising—Hebrew hearer hears not only sitting on gods but potential blood-uncleanness (Lev 15). Reader shares Laban’s ignorance whether claim is true or fabricated.
- **Quote:** “Not only can one sit on gods, but such gods can be rendered unclean if they are stained by Rachel’s blood. The gods, so crucial to Laban, are reduced to ‘sanitary towels,’ or at least a soft cushion”
- **Locus:** on 31:33–35; slice ~L182–186
- **Targets:** [[rachel]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R4-10 | Jacob’s apologia; *rîḇ* bilateral; *paḥaḏ yiṣḥāq* as “Dreaded One of Isaac”
- **Claim:** Jacob’s counter-charge is bilateral dispute, not third-party lawsuit. Twenty years of faithful shepherding; restitution for losses; heat/frost. God as “Dreaded One of Isaac” (*paḥaḏ yiṣḥāq*)—Hamilton prefers traditional “dread” (Ebla name, Job 4:14) over Albright “Kinsman,” Kopf “Refuge,” etc.; meaning **“the One of Isaac who inspires dread”** (source of dread), fitting the dream that restrained Laban. God has judged; Laban plaintiff becomes criminal.
- **Quote:** “If one understands paḥaḏ yişḥāq as ‘the Dreaded One of Isaac,’ does it mean ‘the One whom Isaac dreads,’ or ‘the One of Isaac who inspires dread’? Two points argue for the latter.” / “Laban, originally the plaintiff, has become the criminal. Jacob, originally the criminal, has become the plaintiff.”
- **Locus:** on 31:36–42; slice ~L213–242
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[divine-providence]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-11 | Mizpah/Galeed covenant: two monuments, nonaggression; Laban’s irony
- **Claim:** Against simple J/E split of two meals/two names/two monuments, Hamilton holds unity as etiology of **Mizpah of Gilead** (stele = Mizpah; mound = Gilead) and as signaling Laban’s tacit recognition of Jacob as equal social entity. Laban claims false proprietorship (v. 43); proposes pact lest Jacob mistreat daughters or take other wives—ironic given Laban’s history of mistreating Jacob. God as *watchman* (*ṣāpâ*) and justicer (*šāpaṭ*). Jacob alone takes oath by Dreaded One of Isaac; silent treatment toward Laban. Sacrifice then meal; *lehem* fulfills 28:20 bread prayer physically—return home still incomplete.
- **Quote:** “The unity of the pericope may be maintained if we understand the story as one that tries to explain the origin of the compound place name Mizpah of Gilead.” / “Laban, who time and time again has mistreated Jacob, now solicits a promise from Jacob that he will not mistreat Leah and Rachel. The irony of his request escapes Laban.” / “God will ‘watch’ (sapâ, v. 49) and now he will maintain justice (sapat).”
- **Locus:** on 31:43–54; slice ~L276–300
- **Targets:** [[covenant]], [[jacob]], [[rachel]], [[leah]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-V2R4-12 | Mahanaim: silent *malʾăḵê ʾĕlōhîm*; dual “two camps”
- **Claim:** After Laban’s cold farewell (kiss/bless daughters, not Jacob), Jacob meets **messengers of God**—parallel to Bethel angels (28:12); *pāgaʿ be* stresses unexpectedness; same name-formula as Bethel. **Missing:** any divine speech, panic, or Jacob’s anxiety speech. “Mahanaim” (“two camps”) not fully explained by Jacob’s singular “God’s encampment is this”; may balance “two camps” of v. 8 later. Site later political capital (Ishbosheth, David, Solomon’s district).
- **Quote:** “What is missing from 32:1-3 is any speech from God or his representatives like that at Bethel (28:13-15). The divine messengers encounter Jacob but say nothing. They are just there, silent.”
- **Locus:** on 32:1–3 [Eng. 31:55–32:2]; slice ~L321–334
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R4-13 | Messengers to Esau; Seir/Edom lexical recall of fraternal tensions
- **Claim:** Jacob’s *malʾāḵîm* to Esau mirror God’s; purpose is to mollify. Destination phrase **Seir / country / Edom** recalls Esau’s hairiness, field-man identity, and redness—three sources of tension: birth, birthright, blessing. Jacob’s fear of reprisal is natural misapprehension; neither Esau nor later Joseph is bent on retaliation (cf. 50:15).
- **Quote:** “The three words recall three sources of tension between the brothers — birth, birthright, and blessing.” / “Jacob’s apprehensions turn out to be misapprehensions, as the narrative will indicate.”

### C-V2R4-14 | 400 men, two camps, model prayer
- **Claim:** Messengers’ “on his way to meet you” is ambiguous (hostile or peaceful); four hundred men drive Jacob’s fearful division into two camps (family already “two camps” of Esau-Isaac vs Jacob-Rebekah). Prayer has seven parts; begins and ends quoting God; revises 31:3’s “I will be with you” into “I will treat you well” (*yāṭaḇ* Hiphil—new wording). *qāṭōntî* “I am little/undeserving” echoes younger-son status; rhetoric persuades that God’s interests and Jacob’s coincide.
- **Quote:** “In this prayer Jacob has combined his own circumstances and God’s circumstances into one petition. As such, Jacob’s prayer is ‘a model of rhetoric - a principle of which is to persuade the one appealed to that his interests and one’s own coincide.’”

### C-V2R4-15 | *minḥâ* as voluntary gift; fivefold “face”; propitiate before Peniel
- **Claim:** *minḥâ* here is **gift** not tribute—voluntary, not vassal exacted. ~550 animals, mostly female. Parallel Abigail’s *berāḵâ* to David (1 Sam 25); *minḥâ* is from subservient to superior (God never gives a *minḥâ*). Jacob stays rear; fivefold *pāneh* vocabulary anticipates **Peniel**. ### C-V2R4-16 | Jabbok wrestling: *yaʿăqōḇ / yabbōq / yēʾāḇēq*; “man” → God/angel
- **Claim:** Alone after family crosses Jabbok, Jacob wrestles a **man** (*ʾîš*) until dawn; acoustic cluster *yʿqb/ybq/yʾbq*. *ʾāḇaq* (wrestle) anticipates Esau’s *ḥāḇaq* (embrace, 33:4). Assailant later God (Jacob, v. 31) / angel (Hos 12:5)—mortal inability to recognize divinity until wonder (cf. Gen 18–19; Judg 6; 13). Not a river-demon blocking the ford (no obstacles; fight likely south of Jabbok after crossing).
- **Quote:** “Undoubtedly, there is an acoustical similarity in Jacob (ya‘aqōḇ), Jabbok (yabbōq), and wrestled (yē’āḇēq).” / “The narrator’s use of the term ’îš provides another illustration of the inability of mortals to ascertain the divinity of a supernatural visitor until this visitor performs some wonder.”

- **Claim:** Man strikes/touches (*nāgaʿ be*) hip socket (*kap yĕrēḵô*); possible genital/scrotum reading (cf. Deut 25:11–12) and national import—Israel came from Jacob’s thigh (Exod 1:5). - **Claim:** New name *yiśrāʾēl* explained by *śārîtā* (“you have struggled”) + success with men; original theophoric etymology debated. ### C-V2R4-19 | Peniel: face-to-face; *nṣl* answers prayer; limp + sciatic taboo
- **Claim:** Naming **Peniel** (“face of El”) shifts from struggle-with-man to seeing God face-to-face (immediate presence idiom). “Life preserved” (*nāṣal*) answers earlier “Preserve me from my brother” (v. 12)—assurance Esau will not destroy him. ### C-V2R4-20 | Esau reconciliation: post-Peniel vanguard; *ʾāḇaq*/*ḥāḇaq*; still “uptight Israel”
- **Claim:** Genuine shift: pre-Peniel Jacob stays **behind**; post-Peniel goes **ahead** and bows seven times (reversing 27:29 nations-bow-to-him). Jacob returns *berāḵâ* (v. 11) for stolen blessing—amends without explicit “forgive me.” Yet refusal of escort and **false promise to follow to Seir** show post-Peniel Jacob still capable of subterfuge: not “upright” but **“uptight” Israel**.

### C-V2R4-25 | Simeon/Levi massacre vs brothers’ loot; Jacob’s tactical rebuke; last word
- **Claim (Hamilton’s ethics of the chapter):** On third day Simeon and Levi massacre males, recover Dinah; other sons loot—equal word-counts may mean narrator evaluates killing and looting equally, yet pictures Simeon/Levi as more bold/conscience-driven than “vulture” looters. Levi, Jubilees, Judith) **praise** zeal like Phinehas—paradigm for purity at all costs.

### C-V2R4-26 | Bethel return: bury foreign gods (incl. teraphim); religious maturation
- **Claim:** God commands go up to Bethel, settle, build altar—**only** place God *orders* a patriarch to build an altar. Jacob adds (not in divine command) disposal of **foreign gods**, purification, change of clothes—includes Rachel’s teraphim; parody continues: gods stolen, sat on, blood-stained, **buried** (*ṭāman*, not *qāḇar*). Parallel Josh 24:14; 1 Sam 7:3 renunciation. Marks Jacob’s **religious maturation**—intuits incompatibility with Yahweh. Softens “fleeing Esau” into vague “moment of dire need” when speaking to family.
- **Quote:** “The parody on such gods continues from ch. 31 into ch. 35. Such gods may be stolen, sat on, stained with menstrual blood, and now buried.” / “It is to Jacob’s credit that he himself is responsible for suggesting the extirpation of the gods. … The whole incident must be read as an illustration of Jacob’s religious maturation.”
- **Locus:** on 35:1–4; slice ~L929–947
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[rachel]], [[covenant]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-27 | Terror of God; El-Bethel; Deborah’s death and Rebekah’s absence
- **Claim:** *ḥittat ʾĕlōhîm* protects entourage from pursuit after Shechem—first time others fear Jacob. Renames place **El-Bethel** (“El of the House of El”)—focus on God encountered, not site as residence; ties to fulfilled vow 28:20–21. Deborah’s death: (1) Rebekah never seen again—implied punishment for instigating Isaac’s deception; Jacob undertaker for mother’s nurse; (2) death under oak parallels burial of gods under terebinth; birth-unit (25) / death-unit (35) frame of Jacob cycle. Post-Peniel life is hardship-filled.
- **Quote:** “Presumably she died and was buried before Jacob returned from Aram-naharaim. … Her punishment (implied at least) is that she will never get to see her son again.” / “The opening unit in the Jacob cycle (25:19-34) contains, among its emphases, the birth of two people, Esau and Jacob. The concluding unit in the Jacob cycle (35:1-22) contains, among its emphases, the death of two people, Deborah and Rachel.”
- **Locus:** on 35:5–8; slice ~L964–978
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[esau]], [[rachel]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-V2R4-28 | Second Israel naming as reminder; El Shaddai promises; kings/land
- **Claim:** God *appears* and blesses; renames Jacob→Israel again—not merely rival J/E doublets: briefer reminder to bury “Jacob nature”; name given **before and after** Esau reconciliation so reconciliation is prelude to being truly Israel. El Shaddai: be fruitful—now means **nation/host of tribes and kings**, not more immediate children; land to future descendants. Pillar, oil, unique Genesis libation. Parallels Gen 17 (El Shaddai, name change, kings, God “went up”).
- **Quote:** “Perhaps the repeated bestowal of the new name Israel both before Jacob is reconciled with Esau (ch. 32) and after he is reconciled with Esau (ch. 33) suggests that reconciliation with his estranged brother is a necessary prelude to his becoming truly ‘Israel.’” / “He is not only to bury the foreign gods, but he is to bury what has become for all practical purposes a foreign nature - a Jacob nature.”
- **Locus:** on 35:9–15; slice ~L1034–1055
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[esau]], [[covenant]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R4-29 | Rachel’s death; Ben-oni/Benjamin; Reuben and Bilhah
- **Claim:** Rachel dies in labor near Ephrath/Bethlehem; midwife (not Jacob) consoles—“a son.” Only Jacob-named child; only born in Canaan. **Ben-oni** (“son of my mourning/misfortune” preferred) vs **Benjamin** (“son of the right hand/good fortune”)—Jacob resolves ambiguity; sin-punishment readings (teraphim/oath 31:32) lack explicit support in naming. Pillar on grave “to this day.” Tomb geography (Gen 35 vs 1 Sam 10:2 / Jer 31:15) complicated; Matt 2:18 sides with Bethlehem association. Reuben lies with Bilhah—not mere sex but likely **usurpation** of father’s authority (ANE royal-concubine parallels); Jacob learns but (again) does not strike back.
- **Quote:** “It is ironic that Rachel, who earlier had proclaimed she would die if she had no children (30:1), and who gave to her firstborn the name Joseph, implying a yearning for another son (30:22-24), dies at the birth of this avidly looked-for second son.” / “Is Reuben simply engaging in sexual play? Or, more likely, is he attempting to usurp his father and take control of the family?”
- **Locus:** on 35:16–22a; slice ~L1076–1106
- **Targets:** [[rachel]], [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R4-30 | Twelve sons list; Isaac’s death; Esau and Jacob bury him
- **Claim:** Sons listed by mothers (Leah first)—Dinah again absent. “Born in Paddan-aram” (v. 26b) vs Benjamin in Canaan: source difference or compact genealogy. Isaac dies at 180; if ch. 27 near Esau’s marriages at Isaac’s 100, Isaac lived ~80 more years—“I do not know the day of my death” (27:2) gains irony. Death notice **parallels Abraham’s** (age, *wayyigwaʿ*, gathered to kin, two sons bury, Mamre). Scattered family reunites: Jacob from Ephrath area, Esau from Seir.
- **Quote:** “If he lived for another eighty years or so, he certainly did not know when he would die! … the account of Isaac’s fast-approaching demise is greatly exaggerated. He was wrong about which son was which, and he was equally wrong about how much longer he would live.” / “In many ways the account of Isaac’s death parallels that of his father (25:7-11).”
- **Locus:** on 35:22b–29; slice ~L1132–1144
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[esau]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-V2R4-31 | Edom genealogy purpose: toledot bridge; blessing outside covenant
- **Claim:** Ch. 36’s length shows Bible’s interest in other nations. Pattern: patriarch’s death → *tôlĕdôt* of **older, non-covenant** brother (Ishmael after Abraham; Esau after Isaac) → then *tôlĕdôt* of covenant heir (Isaac; Jacob). Bridge between narrative blocks. Esau’s wives lists conflict with 26:34 / 28:9—harmonization, transmission damage, editorial fluidity, or “unscramble an omelette.” Separation to Seir: livestock pressure like Abraham/Lot—**not hostility**. Outside covenant promise, Esau still receives **children and prosperity**; sometimes appears better than Jacob (amiable departure).
- **Quote:** “In both cases, the death of a patriarch is followed first by a tōleḏôṯ formula that applies to a family that is outside the covenant promise, then by a tōleḏôṯ formula that applies to a family who receives the covenant promise.” / “Although Esau is outside the covenant promise, God’s blessing extends to him in two ways: children (vv. 4-5) and prosperity (vv. 6-7). At some points Esau appears in a better light than Jacob.”
- **Locus:** on 36:1–8; slice ~L1171–1187
- **Targets:** [[esau]], [[jacob]], [[covenant]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R4-32 | Edomite structure: clans, Horites, elective kings, Abrahamic kings?
- **Claim:** Grandsons include Amalek (Timna)—special nomad status vs sedentary Edom. *ʾallûp* = **clan(s)** more than “dukes.” Horite (Seir) genealogy = pre-Edom occupants later dispossessed (Deut 2:12)—conquerors then conquered. King list (36:31–39): eight kings before any king “for Israelites” (pre-Saul or pre-David over Edom)—**elective/nondynastic** (no son succeeds father; different cities); may be sheikh/judge-like contemporaries of Israelite judges. Inclusion may partially fulfill Abraham’s “kings from loins” (17:16) via **non-Israelite Abrahamic** kings; Esau, without Jacob’s 35:11 promise, is associated with eight kings. Final eleven clans: genealogical vs geographical arrangement possible.
- **Quote:** “What is most interesting about the king list is that it reflects an elective kingship rather than a dynastic one.” / “One wonders if the inclusion of this Edomite king list may suggest that the promise to Abraham of kings from his loins (17:16) finds its fulfillment, partially at least, through non-Israelite Abrahamic kings. Jacob also was promised that kings would spring from him (35:11). Esau, who received no such promise, is now associated indirectly with eight kings.”
- **Locus:** on 36:9–43; slice ~L1210–1351
- **Targets:** [[esau]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]], [[victor-hamilton]]
